title: WHY DID JESUS SAY, “PEACE BE WITH YOU” AFTER APPEARING?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS SAY, “PEACE BE WITH YOU” AFTER APPEARING?
The first words the risen Christ spoke to frightened disciples were not “Where were you?” They were words that revealed what the Cross had accomplished.
Imagine being in that room.
The door is locked.
Not because the disciples are having a private worship service.
They are afraid.
Jesus has been crucified. Their Teacher has been publicly humiliated, tortured, and killed. The movement they thought would change everything appears to have collapsed in a matter of hours.
And they know something else.
When Jesus was arrested, they ran.
Peter had insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he never would.
Then the rooster crowed.
Three times Peter had denied even knowing Him.
Now Jesus is dead—or so they had thought—and the disciples are hiding behind locked doors.
Then something happens that changes human history.
Jesus stands among them.
Alive.
Try not to rush past this moment because you already know the ending.
Imagine you were Peter.
Imagine the last meaningful memory you carried of Jesus was the memory of failing Him.
Imagine looking into the face of the Man you abandoned and realizing that the grave could not hold Him.
What would you expect Him to say?
“Where were you?”
“Why did you leave Me?”
“Peter, I warned you.”
“You said you would die with Me.”
Maybe that is what some of us expect God to say when He finally reaches the rooms where we have been hiding.
We know what we did.
We know what nobody else knows.
We remember the prayer we stopped praying.
The temptation we entertained.
The compromise we justified.
The person we wounded.
The secret we buried.
The promise to God we broke.
The version of ourselves everybody sees—and the version only God sees.
So when Jesus walks into the locked room, something inside us expects judgment to be the first sound out of His mouth.
But John records something astonishing.
“Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.”
Eirēnē hymin.
“Peace to you.”

That is the Greek wording preserved in John 20:19: Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν. The noun eirēnē means peace, while hymin means “to you” or “for you.” The wording is therefore naturally rendered, “Peace be with you” or “Peace to you.”
But do not reduce this to Jesus simply saying hello.
Yes, peace was part of the world of Jewish greeting and blessing. But John has carefully prepared us to hear far more in these words.
Before the Cross, Jesus had already told His disciples:
“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” — John 14:27
And later:
“I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace.” — John 16:33
Then comes the Cross.
Then the tomb.
Then resurrection morning.
Then frightened disciples behind locked doors.
And the risen Jesus stands among them and says:
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
Peace to you.
In other words, the peace He promised before Calvary is now spoken by the One who has passed through Calvary and conquered death.
And then Jesus does something that makes the moment even more powerful.
He shows them His wounds.
John places these events together: Jesus says, “Peace to you,” and then shows them His hands and His side. The disciples respond with joy when they recognize the Lord.
Think about that.
Jesus does not announce peace while hiding the scars.
He announces peace and shows them the wounds.
Because Christian peace is not pretending the wound never happened.
Christian peace comes through what Christ accomplished in His suffering, death, and resurrection.
The scars did not disappear when Jesus rose.
But their meaning had changed forever.
They were no longer evidence that death had defeated Him.
They had become the marks carried by the victorious Lamb.
And maybe somebody reading this has scars too.
Some are visible.
Most are not.
A childhood you rarely discuss.
A marriage that shattered.
A betrayal you still replay.
A child you worry about when everyone else is sleeping.
A sin you desperately wish you could undo.
Years wasted running from God.
An addiction nobody knows you are fighting.
A Bible collecting dust while your soul quietly starves.
A smile you have perfected so well that people think you are strong.
You have learned how to walk into church and say, “I’m blessed.”
You have learned how to post the photograph.
Answer the message.
Go to work.
Serve everyone.
Laugh at the right moment.
Then night comes.
The door closes.
And suddenly you are back inside that locked room.
But here is the Gospel:
Locked doors did not keep Jesus away from His frightened disciples.
John explicitly tells us that the doors were shut because the disciples were afraid, yet Jesus came and stood among them.
And perhaps the locked door is exactly where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because human beings still lock doors.
We just became better at hiding the locks.
Pride can be a lock.
Shame can be a lock.
Religion without repentance can be a lock.
Pornography can be a lock.
Bitterness can be a lock.
Success can be a lock.
Church activity can even become a lock when we use ministry to avoid confronting what is happening inside our own hearts.
We hide behind “I’m fine.”
We hide behind “God understands.”
We hide behind “Everybody does it.”
We hide behind “At least I’m not as bad as them.”
But the risen Christ does not merely come to make frightened sinners comfortable in locked rooms.
He comes bringing peace that cost Him blood.
This is where we must understand what biblical peace actually means.
Peace with God is not God deciding sin was never serious.
The Cross tells us precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God cannot be achieved by positive thinking, religious performance, moral comparison, or self-improvement.
Scripture says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Paul says that because we have been justified by faith, “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).
And Colossians describes Christ as making peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).
There is the heart of it.
The peace spoken in that locked room stands on the other side of a bloodstained Cross.
Jesus can stand before guilty, frightened, failed disciples and speak peace because He has accomplished what they could never accomplish for themselves.
He does not call evil good.
He bears sin.
He does not pretend rebellion does not matter.
He provides reconciliation.
He does not tell sinners to save themselves.
He saves.
This is grace.
And grace is far more scandalous than sentimental Christianity makes it sound.
Grace means Peter's failure was real...
but it would not have the final word.
Grace means the disciples really did run...
but Jesus came looking for them.
Grace means the Cross exposes the horror of sin while simultaneously revealing the staggering love of God.
Grace does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your sin mattered so much that Christ died—and His mercy is greater than everything you bring to Him in repentance and faith.”
That is why the Gospel is not a story about good people earning their way to God.
It is the announcement that God acted in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But the story becomes even more astonishing.
Jesus says it again.
“Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.”
“Peace to you.”
Then:
“καθὼς ἀπέσταλκέν με ὁ πατήρ, κἀγὼ πέμπω ὑμᾶς.”
“As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”
The Greek text of John places Christ's repeated declaration of peace immediately alongside His sending of the disciples.
Do you see the movement?
Fear.
Jesus.
Peace.
Wounds.
Joy.
Peace again.
Mission.
The men hiding from the world are about to be sent into it.
The frightened become witnesses.
The scattered become sent.
The ashamed receive a mission.
Jesus does not merely restore their emotional stability.
He gives their lives direction.
That means resurrection peace is not permission to hide forever.
Jesus brings peace into the room...
and then sends His people out of it.
Some of us want the first “Peace be with you” without hearing what follows the second.
We want Jesus to calm us.
Heal us.
Forgive us.
Restore us.
Comfort us.
And He does.
But then He says, in effect:
Now go.
Tell them.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
Grace received becomes grace proclaimed.
Forgiven people become witnesses to forgiveness.
Those who have encountered the risen Christ carry the news of the risen Christ.
That is why sharing the Gospel matters.
Not because clicking “share” earns God's favor.
It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
But when grace has genuinely gripped your heart, you begin wanting somebody else to hear what rescued you.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list is sitting behind a locked emotional door tonight.
Maybe the friend who constantly jokes is quietly falling apart.
Maybe the relative who stopped going to church believes God would never take them back.
Maybe somebody who follows you is one night away from giving up on their faith.
Maybe an unbelieving friend has never actually heard Christianity explained as something more than “try to become a better person.”
Sharing one Christ-centered article cannot save anyone.
Jesus saves.
But God can use a shared testimony, a Scripture passage, a conversation, an invitation, or an article to put truth in front of someone who desperately needs to hear it.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to purchase a blessing.
Not to prove that you are a “real Christian.”
Jesus Christ still enters rooms filled with fear.
Send this to the believer who thinks their failure disqualified them forever.
Send it to the prodigal.
Send it to the skeptic willing to listen.
Send it to the Christian who is exhausted from pretending.
Because eventually, most of us find ourselves behind another locked door.
And when that day comes, you may need to remember what Jesus said when He entered the first one.
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
Peace to you.
Maybe you need to become honest before God right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become more spiritual.
Now.
If you have been hiding something, you do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
Somebody reading your words may discover that they are not the only person who has cried behind a locked door.
This is what Christian community should look like.
Not perfect people performing perfection.
Redeemed sinners pointing one another toward a perfect Savior.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus paid the price.
Your response to that Gospel is repentance and faith in Him.
And perhaps that is why His first words in that room remain so breathtaking.
The disciples had failed Him.
Yet He came.
They were afraid.
Yet He came.
The doors were locked.
Yet He came.
They had nothing with which to impress Him.
Yet He came.
And He stood among them carrying wounds that testified both to the terrible cost of sin and the immeasurable depth of His love.
Then He spoke:
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
Peace to you.
Maybe you thought peace would come when your circumstances finally changed.
When the anxiety disappeared.
When the family healed.
When the money arrived.
When the temptation vanished.
When everybody apologized.
When you finally forgave yourself.
But the disciples discovered something better.
Peace entered the room because Jesus entered the room.
The risen Christ Himself was their peace.
And the deepest Christian hope is not that Jesus promises us a life without wounds.
It is that the One who still bore His wounds walked out of His grave.
Your scars are not your Savior.
Your shame is not your master.
Your failure does not get to sit on the throne.
Death itself does not get the last sentence.
Jesus Christ does.
So unlock what you have been hiding.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent where you need to repent.
Receive the mercy Christ offers.
Return if you have wandered.
And when His grace has found you again, do not keep the news trapped behind a locked door.
And comment.
Tell us what Christ is healing.
Tell us what you are surrendering.
Tell us where you need prayer.
Because somebody else may be hiding in the same darkness you survived.
The disciples thought the locked room was where their story was ending.
Jesus walked in and turned it into the room from which they would be sent.
Never mistake the room where fear locked you in for the place where Jesus intends to leave you.
